$comment: THE LEDGER (#159). /resources/ is defined as one article per useful learning —
the operator's words, 24 Aug 2026: "we should create one article per useful
learning under /resources or /blog on the website". #144 shipped the section and
a fixed list of nine articles. A fixed list cannot be checked, so it drifts: a
learning enters the research, nobody writes it up, and nothing goes red.
This file is the list the section is derived from. Every row is one learning and
every row carries a verdict. `test/learnings.test.js` enforces both directions:
a row with verdict `article` must name an article that exists and that declares
this row's id in its `learnings:` frontmatter, and an article may not declare an
id this file does not carry. A `not-publishable` row must carry a written reason.
Nothing here counts articles or rows — writing more never turns the suite red.
WHAT IS NOT CHECKED, said plainly: this repo cannot see the research. A learning
entered here is the one drift no test can catch. Adding the row is the job of the
thread that adds the learning; `ref` is what makes the row findable in the source.

scope: Parts 1, 3, 5, 8 and 9 — the diagnostic instruments, what Prospektor hands its
clients, the SFTROU doctrine, channels and founder-led sales, and churn. These
are the parts that contain findings a reader could act on.
Parts 2, 4, 6 and 7 are out of scope and deliberately carry no rows: they are
Prospektor's own growth diagnosis, its product roadmap, its four-week plan and
its AI-era strategic argument. None is a finding about finding or winning a
customer, which is what this section is for. Promote a row out of them the day
one turns out to be — the rule is the reader, not the part number.
PROMOTED, 31 Aug 2026 (#446/#447): build-to-save-is-a-rounding-error, out of
§7.1. It is the first row taken from an out-of-scope part, under the rule
immediately above, and it qualifies on the reader test rather than by
exception — a founder deciding what to run their own sales on is deciding
how to win a customer, and the arithmetic is theirs to apply, not this
company's. Part 7 is otherwise what the scope note says it is: a strategic
argument about where this business sits, which is not a finding for a reader.
PROMOTED, 7 Sep 2026 (#447): learn-a-channel-fast and direct-mail-needs-the-acv
out of §7.6, and job-not-persona out of §7.5 — the last three spoke-sized
findings on the founder-led sales term, and the reason the cluster closes at
four pieces (ROADMAP.md, #447, 7 Sep). Each qualifies on the reader test: how
to get competent at a channel, whether a channel's price can carry it, and
what to segment a prospect list on are all decisions a founder takes to win a
customer. Nothing else in Part 7 is, and it stays out.

learnings.title: The MRR ceiling is new MRR divided by churn — a hard cap, computable today
Walling runs the same ceiling calculation as Cohen, independently — it is the field's consensus arithmetic, not one person's heuristic
The churn benchmark ladder, average lifetime = 1 ÷ monthly churn, and how fast a cohort disappears at 10%
Powers-of-ten market sizing kills a bad segment in four minutes instead of four months
Total Reachable Market, not Total Addressable — how many you can get in front of with the channels you have
Size the segment by powers of ten before touching it — pitch quality cannot rescue arithmetic
Forever customers build you into something they sell; temporary customers should not be allowed to set your spending
Prefer prospects who will resell you rather than consume you once
A one-time-use product is a top-three cause of early plateau — and the fix is the cohort, not the price
The retention curve must flatten and hold, not decay to zero, or cohorts never layer
"Too expensive" is never the real cancellation reason — they already agreed the price when they bought
Requested features are table stakes; delight comes from you, and customers are not product people
Position to the buyer's career, not the buyer's task — and the Slack-channel test for whether it is strong enough
Lead with what it does for the human, not the org — a career claim beats a utility claim
The 3× bar: a 20–30% improvement does not move anyone, and saving money is a much weaker pitch than making it possible
Ads bought to learn the words, not to buy the customers — time-boxed, with copy as the deliverable
Affinity is not a channel — spend where your buyers are, with a budgeted column for what you love
The big five B2B approaches, the selection question, and which ad platform each kind of targeting knowledge licenses
Cohort quality beats cohort size — pick the pond where the fish jump in the boat
The best segment is where a client's happiest, longest-retained customers already cluster
A new motion nobody owns gets eaten by the existing business, every time
A week is not enough and six months is too long — and the comfortable work is what kills the experiment
2-2-200: two hours of research, twenty of conversations, two hundred of building — in that order
Building more does not de-risk the company; it defers the moment you find out
Target the buyer for whom this is a top-two priority this quarter, not the company that could want it
If they would not want it free — free of money and of their time — it is a no, not a slow deal
A prospect who has staffed the problem is a harder sale, and the pitch has to change from replace to capacity
Lost-to-competitor and no-decision look identical in a CRM and demand opposite fixes
Nobody takes a meeting to be sold to — the reply-rate ceiling is set by how much of the list is in-market
This person at this company did this thing and this happened — generic capability claims are the failure mode
Angle, Reason, Example, Angle — how to answer a hard question on a call while you are still thinking
Merge-tag personalisation costs trust; showing someone their own stuff buys it
Send the artefact instead of asking for the meeting in which you would describe it
The cold email to an activated buyer, and why each line is there
The four-email sequence whose first email expects roughly no replies
Mentioning price on the first call closes 40% against 28%
The ten-objection document, two hours, answers capped at three sentences — because a long answer concedes the objection
The first call is a sale and a research interview at once, and the research half is what compounds
Known-said, known-unsaid, unknown-unsaid — and why naming level one proves nothing
Make money, save money, increase efficiency, mitigate risk — seven people, four stories, and you must know which to tell to whom
Within one power of ten of their revenue, or answering a public strategic mandate — otherwise it is a wish
Partners want support and a project to sell, not a commission
Give an agency something it can hand its own client under its own name
The highest-ROI email in the set goes to the partners you already have, about the clients they already have
The partner opening: credibility from having done their job, and letting them name the commercial terms
"We already do this in-house" — accept the premise and move the claim to capacity
Account-based or campaign-based is decided by price, and the thresholds are explicit
A few hundred high-value customers beats ten thousand — the maths does not favour scale for a small team
Three practitioners, three floors — below roughly $3–5k ACV, outbound does not pay for itself
A redlined contract, procurement routing or a security questionnaire is a pricing event, not a paperwork event
You will lose 75–85% of first meetings, and a 25% win rate is very good
Visitor-to-trial and trial-to-paid ranges, and what a credit-card gate does to both
104 conversations to 24 sales calls — a 23% conversation-to-call rate as the activity model to copy
An audience gives reach; a network gives leverage — with the three launch numbers that settle it
Fewer than 5% of 210 companies ever built an audience — borrow one instead, ten emails at a time
The newsletter and the excuse to call — how a relationship survives the gap between deals
Niching down wins more customers, not fewer, because clear trade-offs are what let non-ideal buyers buy
Vertical and orthogonal both beat horizontal — and the orthogonal cut costs no code
The minimum is three channels now, and existing off-search makes search itself easier
Use discovery platforms to reduce your dependency on discovery platforms
Cold email and cold LinkedIn are saturating, and the physical alternative only works paired with a trust layer
"How did you hear about us?" moves you from ~55% to 75–80% attributed, and costs nothing
Every channel skill costs about a year — budget one, learned properly
Nothing sales-related leaves the founder below $300k, and the gate is running the full process ten times
Hire two reps or none — one rep gives you an argument, two give you a diagnosis
In person, then calls, then email — most context first, most scale last
The answer to hating sales is a script, not a personality transplant
SEO is five years to anything interesting, plus the cheap structural wins if you do it anyway
learnings.reason: The one operative half — put the blog in a subfolder, slug exactly the keyword — is a build instruction for this site, taken by #144, and the rest waits on #137's audit. It becomes an article the day the section has search data to write against rather than a claim about search.

learnings.title: The Three Factor Framework for prioritising marketing approaches
learnings.reason: The source names it on air and never enumerates it, and third-party summaries disagree about what the three factors are. Publishing a reconstruction would be inventing a framework and attributing it to someone.

learnings.title: Over 90% of SaaS ideas come from proximity; cold research is the least productive origin, at 8%
learnings.reason: It is a finding about finding an idea to build, not about finding customers for a business that already exists — the second is this section's whole remit. Its live warning (aim at operators with a product and a quota, not at founders still looking for an idea) is a targeting decision for this site, not a reader's lesson.

learnings.title: The summary of what Parts 8 settles and leaves open
learnings.reason: A summary of rows that already carry articles, plus Prospektor's own channel choice. Its one novel number, the BlinkMetrics activity model, has its own row.

learnings.title: Rob Walling's twelve commandments
learnings.reason: General founder doctrine — think in spectrums, decide without certainty, overnight success takes a decade. The four load-bearing ones carry their own rows and their own articles; the remainder is not a finding about finding or winning a customer.

learnings.title: The eight classic traps, two of which are on Prospektor's own board
learnings.reason: A build-side checklist read against this company's roadmap. Its live entries are internal decisions on board rows #113 and #114, not advice a reader is in a position to take.

learnings.title: The three categories of AI product, and which one Prospektor is
learnings.reason: A positioning question about this product, argued for this product. The reader-facing half of it — how large a claim has to be before anyone acts on it — is the 3× row, which has an article.

learnings.title: The moat that is not a moat — doing the expensive thing a funded competitor will refuse to do
learnings.reason: A defensibility argument for a company that already has customers, not a finding about getting them. It is also the load-bearing argument in this company's own CLAUDE.md moat audit, which makes it strategy rather than field notes.

learnings.title: Concierge onboarding is indicated above $100/mo or 20 seats, and the barbell that makes the mid-range dangerous
learnings.reason: About activating a customer who has already bought. This section stops at the sale; taking it further would need a second section with its own remit rather than a stray article about onboarding.

learnings.title: Instrument why people cancel: multiple choice not freeform, offer a pause, route by reason
learnings.reason: Post-sale retention mechanics. The one part a seller acts on — that the stated reason is usually not the real one — is the too-expensive article, which has its own row.

learnings.title: The rule of 15, the announced annual increase, and why freemium is not a distribution fix
learnings.reason: Price-book operations for a company with a live subscriber base. What a price licenses you to *do* in sales is the row that has an article; what you charge existing customers next year is not this section's subject.

learnings.title: Expansion revenue is the missing holy grail
learnings.reason: Revenue growth inside accounts you already won. Out of remit for the same reason as concierge onboarding — this section is about the sale, up to and including the moment it closes.

learnings.title: Building a tool to save money is a rounding error against the enterprise value a growing month produces — and the two cases that survive the arithmetic
Learning a channel you have never run: one practitioner, the reading time-boxed to a day or two, the first attempt made badly, then a coach — and an LLM gives the average answer
Direct mail is an account-based motion that needs the annual contract value, cash upfront and annual billing — the early letters are paid for before any of them work
Why they buy is not who they are — segment by the job and the workflow, not the industry or the persona; two independent experts, one conclusion
